title: 2 Samuel 24:15–17
context: The LORD sends a pestilence, and seventy thousand die across the land, but as the angel stretches out his hand toward Jerusalem, the LORD relents and stops him at the threshing floor of Araunah. David, seeing the angel, confesses his sin and asks that God’s hand fall on him and his father’s house rather than the people. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground on God’s judgment, his mercy in relenting, and a king’s intercession for his people.

verses.text: So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel from the morning even to the appointed time; and seventy thousand men died of the people from Dan even to Beersheba.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD sends a pestilence, and seventy thousand die from Dan to Beersheba. Arminian readers treat the deaths soberly as real judgment.

The text gives no further explanation, and no speculation is added.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read the verse with sobriety, seeing God’s judgment fall on Israel, against whom his anger had burned (v. 1).

Both traditions affirm God’s justice while grieving the loss.

verses.text: When the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented of the disaster, and said to the angel who destroyed the people, “It is enough. Now withdraw your hand.” The LORD’s angel was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.
verses.arminianNotes:
As the angel reaches toward Jerusalem, the LORD relents and says, “It is enough.” Arminian readers note God’s responsiveness and mercy (cf. Jer 18:8).

The angel stands by Araunah’s threshing floor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s mercy limiting judgment. They usually read “relented” as describing God’s turning from the disaster within his settled purpose, while Arminian readers often stress his real responsiveness; both affirm his mercy here.

Neither tradition reads this relenting as a change in God’s knowledge or character, a point also made at Judges 10:16 and 1 Samuel 15:29. The location will become the site of the altar.

verses.text: David spoke to the LORD when he saw the angel who struck the people, and said, “Behold, I have sinned, and I have done perversely; but these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me, and against my father’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David says, “I have sinned... but these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me.” Arminian readers note David’s willingness to bear the judgment himself.

He intercedes as a shepherd for his flock.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a king offering himself for his people, which many Christians read as pointing to Christ the good shepherd (John 10:11), as a reading.

Both traditions see genuine intercession here.
